A.evidence: Randomized real data: KuaiRand random exposures, Hillstrom, Criteo, Open Bandit Dataset
A.supports: A component ranks or targets better in that domain; on the Open Bandit Dataset, how close an off-policy estimator comes to a known policy value
A.cannot: Anything about push, fatigue or long-term effects

B.evidence: Off-policy estimate on real logs from an estimator first validated against a known answer
B.supports: The value of a new policy within the support of the logging policy
B.cannot: Policies outside that support; long horizons

C.evidence: Simulator runs with a sensitivity sweep
C.supports: Policy A beats B across a stated share of assumptions, or flips at a stated threshold

history.evidence: A registered verdict later overturned by a larger check
history.supports: Nothing beyond the record of the verdict

descriptive.evidence: Counts of a fixed set, no inference

note: The project has no Tier B result: no estimator passed the check on the full Men's campaign of OBD, the only real logs with two policies and known propensities here.

The estimator IPS, on real randomized logs (full Men's campaign of OBD), estimates the BTS click rate at this fraction of its on-policy value. The target is BTS with its fixed prior, which the deployed BTS was not, so the shortfall may come from the estimator or from that mismatch, and these data do not separate the two (post_hoc_empirical_target re-weights to the BTS logs' own frequencies; post_hoc_difference is its paired change from this ratio, with an interval that includes 0). Post hoc reading: the small sample has too little power to show the shortfall
